cues.text: From Slave to Deacon
Callistus began life as the household slave of a Christian named Carpophorus, entrusted with running a bank on his master's behalf.
When the bank failed, Callistus fled Rome, was caught, and was condemned to hard labor in the mines of Sardinia — a common death sentence in all but name, given the brutal conditions.
He was freed through the intercession of Pope St. Victor I, who arranged for his release along with other Christian prisoners.
On his return to Rome, his predecessor Pope Zephyrinus made the remarkable choice to ordain him a deacon and entrust him with the Church's affairs.
Keeper of the Catacombs
As deacon, Callistus was placed in charge of the official Christian burial ground on the Appian Way, thereafter known as the Catacomb of Callistus .
It became the burial place of numerous popes and remains one of the largest and most important early Christian cemeteries in Rome.
His administration of Church property and charity under Zephyrinus made him the natural, if controversial, choice to succeed him as bishop of Rome around 217 or 218.
Controversy and Mercy
Callistus's pontificate was marked by sharp internal conflict.
He extended reconciliation to Christians who had committed serious sins, including adultery and murder, after due penance.
This mercy outraged theological rigorists led by the priest Hippolytus , who denounced Callistus as too lax and set himself up as a rival bishop, becoming the Church's first recorded antipope.
Hippolytus's own polemical writings, though hostile, are one of the chief surviving sources for Callistus's life.
A Quiet Reign, A Violent End
Callistus governed during a period of relative peace under Emperor Alexander Severus, whose own mother had Christian sympathies.

The Catholic Encyclopedia notes that an oratory Callistus had built was, in one dispute with tavern-keepers over the property, protected by imperial ruling that any devotional use of the site should be respected.
Despite this general toleration, Callistus was killed in a local riot around 222, thrown from a window into a well in Trastevere.
The ancient Depositio Martirum of the fourth century remembered his death as true martyrdom, even though it fell short of formal state persecution.
Legacy
Callistus is remembered as the earliest pope listed as a genuine martyr in the Church's oldest surviving liturgical calendars.
His willingness to readmit serious sinners to communion after penance — over the objections of rigorist critics — anticipated the Church's enduring pastoral practice of mercy toward the repentant.
The catacomb that bears his name remains, to this day, one of the great physical witnesses to the faith of the earliest Roman Christians.
